source_text: Verum his ut res postulabat impletis, iuvat te vel mediocriter convenire, qua fiducia tu, cum Hieronymi scripta collaudes, dicas in Christo non fuisse peccatum, cum ille in Dialogo illo, quem sub nomine Attici et Critoboli, mira et ut talem fidem decebat venustate composuit, etiam quinti Evangelii [n125] , quod a se translatum dicit, testimonio nitatur ostendere, Christum non solum naturale, verum etiam voluntarium habuisse peccatum, propter quod se cognoverit Ioannis baptismate diluendum. De alio etiam testimonio Ioannis evangelistae, flagitium ei assuit falsitatis [n126] . De quo opere tu in illa epistola, quam Alexandriam destinasti, ita gloriaris, ut dicas Pelagium, Scripturarum ab eo oppressum molibus, arbitrium liberum vindicare non posse. Verum illi operi a catholico viro, qui pulsatus fuerat, obviatum est. Nunc vero ad hoc commemorationem eius tantummodo feci, ut te recognosceres non solum Scripturis sanctis, sed nec ipsis tui dogmatis adiutoribus consonare.
pass_a_gloss: But these things having been fulfilled as the matter demanded, it pleases to convene you even moderately, by what confidence you, when you praise Jerome's writings, say there was not sin in Christ, when he in that Dialogue which under the names of Atticus and Critobulus he composed with a wonderful charm and such as became such a faith, strives to show even by the testimony of a fifth Gospel, which he says was translated by himself, that Christ had not only natural but even voluntary sin, on account of which he knew himself to be washed by John's baptism. From another testimony also of John the evangelist he sews onto him the outrage of falsehood. About which work you in that letter which you sent to Alexandria so glory that you say Pelagius, oppressed by the masses of the Scriptures from him, cannot vindicate free decision. But that work was met by a catholic man who had been struck. Now however I have made commemoration of it only for this, that you may recognize that you agree not only not with the holy Scriptures, but not even with the very helpers of your dogma.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Having completed these points as the subject required, I would like to question you at least briefly. With what confidence do you say there was no sin in Christ while praising Jerome’s writings? In that Dialogue he composed under the names Atticus and Critobulus, with a remarkable elegance befitting such a faith, he even relies on the testimony of a fifth Gospel, which he says he translated, to try to show that Christ had not only natural but even voluntary sin, because of which he knew he needed cleansing by John’s baptism (compare Jerome, Dialogue against the Pelagians 3.1). From another testimony of John the evangelist, he also fastens on Christ the disgrace of falsehood (compare Jerome, Dialogue against the Pelagians 2.6; John 7:8–10). In the letter you sent to Alexandria, you boast of this work so much that you say Pelagius, overwhelmed by its masses of Scripture, cannot defend free choice. But that work was answered by the catholic man who had been attacked. I have now mentioned it only to make you recognize that you agree neither with the holy Scriptures nor even with the helpers of your own doctrine.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
